OK Cancel Back to top Image: Bigstock Stock Market News for Oct 13, 2026 Read More Hide Full Article Wall Street closed mixed on Monday, driven by a rise in energy stocks. Investor mood was grim on oil prices jumping nearly $2 per barrel after Middle East escalations. An important Fed official said that the U.S. central bank should move relatively quickly to a more restrictive monetary policy. One of the three benchmark indexes ended in the green, while two ended in the red. How Did the Benchmarks Perform? The Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJI) added 195.6 points, or 0.4%, to close at 51,850.55. Twenty components of the 30-stock index ended in positive territory, while 10 ended in negative. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite lost 120.27 points, or 0.4%, to close at 27,245.9. The S&P 500 slid 4.3 points, or 0.1%, to close at 7,807.24. Eight of the 11 broad sectors of the benchmark index closed in the green. The Energy Select Sector SPDR (XLE), the Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR (XLP) and the Communication Services Select Sector SPDR (XLC) advanced 1.5%, 1.2% and 1.1%, respectively, while the Technology Select Sector SPDR (XLK) declined 0.9%. The fear gauge CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) increased 2.5% to 15.21. A total of 12.7 billion shares were traded on Monday, lower than the last 20-session average of 17.6 billion. Decliners outnumbered advancers by a 1.09-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 1.59-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. Saudi Airport Attacks Lift Oil Prices, Hurt Investor Sentiment Fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia heightened concerns over Middle East security, pushing oil prices higher and dampening investor confidence. Saudi authorities reported that one person was killed and 11 others injured after an unidentified projectile struck Terminal 4 at Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday, triggering a fire. The incident followed a Houthi-claimed attack a day earlier that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300. The escalating violence raised concerns about potential disruptions to regional energy supplies, overshadowing expectations of increased availability. U.S. President Donald Trump welcomed additional Russian diesel exports and a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire covering energy targets, but these developments failed to ease upward pressure on crude prices. Brent crude futures gained $1.93, or 1.8%, to settle at $106.65 per barrel, marking their highest close since Sept. 15. West Texas Intermediate crude advanced $1.89, or 2%, to $93.74. Rising energy costs and geopolitical uncertainty weighed on Wall Street investor mood, renewing concerns about inflation, corporate expenses and the potential implications for interest rates. Consequently, ConocoPhillips ( COP Quick Quote COP - Free Report )     and ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation ( XOM Quick Quote XOM - Free Report )     gained 2.6% and 1.9%, respectively. While COP currently boasts a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), XOM carries a Rank #3 (Hold). You can see the complete list of today's Zacks #1 Rank stocks here. Fed’s Hammack Urges Swift Action to Curb Persistent Inflation Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack called for the Fed to tighten monetary policy relatively quickly, warning that inflation is spreading beyond energy and influencing companies’ pricing strategies. She estimated underlying inflation in the mid-to-high 2% range and expects a gradual return to the Fed’s 2% target. Rising costs for technology components, partly driven by AI infrastructure investment, are adding pressure across data centers, aviation, electricity and construction. Hammack favored smaller, timely policy adjustments over potentially larger moves later. Traders have raised the probability of an October hike to nearly 22%, from 17.7% on Friday, according to CME’s FedWatch tool. No economic data was released on Monday. Add us on Google Add us on Google As of 7:45 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil is trading at $107.29 per barrel, based on the Brent benchmark we’ll explain in a bit. That’s 75 cents below yesterday morning’s level and about $44 higher than where it stood a year ago. Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $108.04 -0.69% Price of oil 1 month ago $106.02 +1.19% Price of oil 1 year ago $63.69 +68.45% Price of oil yesterday Oil price per barrel $108.04 % Change -0.69% Price of oil 1 month ago Oil price per barrel $106.02 % Change +1.19% Price of oil 1 year ago Oil price per barrel $63.69 % Change +68.45% Will oil prices go up? No one can say for sure where oil prices will go next. Many forces shape the market—but at the core, it’s still about supply and demand. When risks like a potential recession or war ramp up, oil prices can change direction quickly. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices When you buy gas at the pump, you’re covering more than the cost of crude oil. You’re also paying for every step in the process, including refineries, wholesalers, taxes, and the markup your local gas station adds. Even so, crude oil has the biggest influence on what you pay, often making up more than half the cost per gallon. When oil prices jump, gas prices usually climb right along with them. But when oil falls, gas prices often slip much more slowly—a pattern sometimes called “rockets and feathers.” The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve If an emergency hits, the U.S. keeps a backup supply of crude oil called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It’s mainly there to protect energy security during crises, such as sanctions, catastrophic storm damage, even war. It can also help cushion the blow when supply shocks send prices soaring. It’s not meant to solve long-term problems. Instead, it provides quick relief for consumers and helps keep vital parts of the economy moving, like essential industries, emergency services, and public transit. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Oil and natural gas are two of the world’s primary energy sources. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which which increases demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil When looking at how oil performs, two main benchmarks stand out: Brent crude oil is the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is the main benchmark of North America. Of the two, Brent gives a better picture of global oil performance because it prices a large share of the world’s traded crude. It’s also the go-to for tracking oil’s historical trends. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now relies on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. If you look at the Brent benchmark over several decades, oil has been far from stable. It has experienced sharp rises tied to wars and supply cuts, along with steep drops linked to global recessions and oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s delivered the first major oil shock when the Middle East slashed exports and placed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices fell in the mid-1980s due to lower demand and an influx of non-OPEC oil producers joining the market. Prices surged again in 2008 as global demand grew, but then crashed alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand plummeted like never before—pushing prices below $20 per barrel. To sum up, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s heavily influenced by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, shifting energy policies, and much more. Check out our recent coverage: Delta’s CEO says those higher ticket prices could be here to stay as long as demand holds up Zelenskyy: Russia striking Ukraine’s energy facilities despite Trump’s ceasefire claim The IEA wants to empty its oil reserves faster Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.
